name: Late-Night Foodie (André & Sofia archetype)
tagline: The post-midnight brisket run is a ritual — and I'll bring the whole crew, if I can just find the truck.
one_liner: A food-culture-driven 20-something out late off a bar shift or after a venue, for whom the post-midnight quality-taco run is a ritual. A genuine taco nerd and organic amplifier who converts the crew — held back only by not knowing which truck is open, and where, at the exact hour the craving peaks.

demographics.Occupation: Service industry (bartender, line cook) / creative nightlife (DJ, crew)

quote: I'm doing their marketing for free at 1am, bro — and happily. But the number one reply I always get is 'where.' Everyone can see it's incredible; it's 'where do I get it.'

items.text: Cap the night with real food, not a regret — after eight hours on their feet, the post-shift/after-venue taco run is an earned ritual, not just a meal.
Be the one who runs the table — convening coworkers and the venue crowd, ordering across the menu so everyone tastes everything, and converting sceptics on the spot.
Champion fusion done right — evangelising a brisket and Korean-chicken taco whose flavours genuinely make sense, not a gimmick, as a badge of taste.
Be in the know — access and insider status matter more than points; being first to the drop is the real reward.
Comes off shift between 12:30 and 2:30am and rolls up as a pack — leads the group order, splits everything, and personally drags in coworkers, touring bands, DJs.
Posts nearly every visit — the unwrap, the steam, the truck lights behind the taco — as stories and the occasional TikTok, generating a wave of replies.
Orders the smoked brisket as a baseline and puts the salsa verde on everything — deep, specific menu knowledge that makes the enthusiasm persuasive.
Runs an informal 'intelligence network' to locate the truck late — DMing the local account, texting friends, cross-referencing before committing to the walk.
Word of mouth within the scene is the real signal — a trusted person saying 'no, actually, go' outweighs any ad, especially at 2am when nobody is searching.
TikTok and Instagram — close-up brisket and first-bite clips — are the visual confirmation that makes the recommendation feel real.
Acts as an amplifier, not just a follower: their own posts drive a stream of 'where is this?' replies, seeding new demand from the scene.
Cannot confirm which truck is open or where, late, when trucks relocate to venues and clubs — the single biggest barrier, turning a 20-minute walk into an empty corner.
The app's 'open now' is no longer trusted and its static menu doesn't match the truck board, so the highest-intent user checks it 'like a weather app I don't believe.'
A dormant local Instagram reads as closed even when the truck is out — 'you lose to certainty, not to quality' — so ready-to-spend intent goes to the place known to be open.
For the Montreal francophone, an English-only national presence reads as 'not made for here' — a small but real exclusion that cools the relationship.

blocks.title: What would deepen the relationship & drive subscription

items.text: Late-night location drops above all — a 'we're parked at Richmond & Portland till 3am tonight' alert — framed as service, not marketing; would sign up in a heartbeat.
Insider / creator access — location drops and seasonal previews first, early notice of a Fuego Nights return — 'crew energy, not punch-card energy.'
Bilingual done properly in authentic fr-CA; English-only loyalty content is an instant unsubscribe, and translated-from-France copy is worse than English.
Skip the opaque points scheme — access beats discounts, and a friend-in-the-scene register beats three 'ORDER NOW' pushes a day.
Conversion: the first midnight brisket taco is a jolt of delight — real smoke, real technique at 1am — that turns a hungry regular into an evangelist.
Frustration on the hunt: intent and appetite are high, but not being able to confirm the truck is there leaves them 'mad and still hungry' — a lost sale from a superfan.
Willing amplifier waiting to be armed: doing the word of mouth for free, out of genuine affection, and asking only that the brand meet them halfway — 'tell us where the truck is.'
